title: Beauty In My Backyard - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: Architectural ugliness is not what drives local (NIMBY) opposition to housing — restrictive zoning arrived in the 1890s-1920s, a generation before modernism — but it did create a mass constituency of distant, casually motivated 'NITBYs' who powered the 1960s-70s heritage conservation movement. Because historic stock is concentrated in the most economically valuable city centers, conservation now freezes redevelopment exactly where land is most valuable, pushing density to peripheral sites like La Défense and producing 'L transect' skylines in the New World.

themes.theme: NIMBY vs NITBY: a new taxonomy of development opposition

insights.claim: Opposition to development splits into two distinct constituencies: 'NIMBYs' who live near a scheme and object on grounds of disruption, green space, services and social exclusivity, and 'NITBYs' ('Not in that backyard') who live nowhere near it and object because they judge it makes the country uglier.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Political risk models for housing projects should be split by constituency: sweeteners that pacify neighbors (compensation, infrastructure) do nothing against NITBYs, who are only moved by design quality.
insights.quote: The first group are often called ‘NIMBYs’, for ‘Not in my backyard’. Let us call the second group ‘NITBYs’, for ‘Not in that backyard’.
insights.locator: Western countries used to let landowners build

insights.claim: Most distant opponents of development are only casually interested and altruistically motivated, asking merely whether a scheme is a cursory objective improvement to its neighborhood — yet this diffuse, low-intensity support aggregates into a decisive political force in a democracy.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Diffuse aesthetic sentiment is a latent veto that does not show up in local consultation headcounts; developers underprice this tail risk on visually prominent central sites.
insights.quote: Their motives are faint but basically altruistic: their question is whether or not, based on a cursory assessment, a development is an objective improvement to its neighborhood.
insights.locator: While a few NITBYs are fervent campaigners

insights.claim: The heritage conservation movement displays the priority profile of a distant-observer movement rather than a homeowner movement: it protects working-class housing, commercial downtowns, public buildings, isolated country houses and rural churches, categories in which self-interested local homeowners have no stake.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Conservation constraints will keep binding in commercial and post-industrial districts where there is no resident base to negotiate with — a distinct risk category from suburban zoning.
insights.quote: In other words, the conservation movement has the priorities of a NITBY movement, not a NIMBY one.
insights.locator: The pretextual theory also struggles to explain

insights.claim: Beauty is not a panacea for local opposition: I'On in Charleston, South Carolina, one of the loveliest neighborhoods in North America, drew thousands of petition signatures, an initial town council rejection and a downzoning referendum, and was only saved when the South Carolina Supreme Court ruled that zoning decisions cannot be made by referendum.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Design-led placemaking does not de-risk entitlement; legal precedent on referendum-based zoning is a more reliable protection than aesthetic quality.
insights.quote: The NIMBYs were defeated only after the South Carolina Supreme Court found that zoning decisions cannot be made by referendum.
insights.locator: I’On (pronounced ‘ion’) in Charleston

insights.claim: The Duchy of Cornwall's proposed South East Faversham scheme in Kent — potentially one of the most appealing urban extensions in modern Europe, from the team behind Poundbury and Nansledan — has still triggered hundreds of protest letters plus opposition from Faversham Council, neighboring councils and the local MP.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Even royal patronage plus proven traditional design does not clear UK planning risk; underwrite British land options on legal/political process, not on design merit.
insights.quote: Nonetheless, it has triggered hundreds of letters of protest, as well as opposition from Faversham Council, the neighboring councils, and the local Member of Parliament.
insights.locator: The present king of the United Kingdom is an architecture enthusiast

themes.theme: Sequencing evidence: zoning preceded modernism by a generation

insights.claim: Restrictive zoning emerged in Germany and Austria-Hungary in the 1890s, reached Italian cities in the 1900s, Britain in 1909 and France in 1919, then spread across the United States in the interwar period — decades before modernist architecture became dominant.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The regulatory freeze on Western land supply is over a century old and predates any aesthetic grievance — expect it to be structurally sticky rather than fixable by design reform.
insights.quote: Restrictive zoning emerged in Germany and Austria-Hungary in the 1890s and spread quickly thereafter.
insights.locator: A more powerful reason to doubt the role of ugliness

insights.claim: In Germany and Austria most suburbs were capped at their existing densities well before 1914 and still retain those densities today, meaning more than a century of frozen suburban land use.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: German and Austrian suburban land carries near-zero density optionality; upside must come from statutory reform, not from local negotiation.
insights.quote: in Germany and Austria most suburbs were capped at their existing densities well before 1914, and retain those densities today
insights.locator: The restrictiveness of early zoning varied by country

insights.claim: Modernist architecture emerged in Germany in the 1920s, remained a minority futurist style in the 1930s, had particularly faint impact in the United States — whose famous 1930s-40s buildings like the Supreme Court Building, Empire State Building and Jefferson Memorial stayed Neoclassical or Art Deco — and only triumphed globally in the 1950s.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Anchors the timeline that breaks the popular 'ugly buildings caused zoning' story — a useful correction for anyone modeling policy causation in housing.
insights.quote: The global triumph of modernism came only in the 1950s.
insights.locator: Modernist architecture began at least a generation later

insights.claim: The Great Downzoning happened while the buildings being banned were still traditional — classical cornices, pedimented windows, rusticated basements — so restrictive land-use rules cannot have been a reaction to perceived ugliness.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Directly undercuts the 'build beautiful and supply will follow' policy thesis that many housing reform advocates and design-led developers rely on.
insights.quote: The flats that were banned by early zoning would generally have had classical cornices, pedimented windows, and rusticated basements.
insights.locator: This means that the Great Downzoning happened

insights.claim: Visual preference surveys consistently find that most people prefer traditional architectural styles to modernist ones, making modernism a demonstrably unpopular style rather than merely a contested taste.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Measurable public preference is an exploitable asymmetry: traditional-style schemes face less diffuse opposition even if they face equal local opposition.
insights.quote: visual preference surveys consistently find that most people prefer traditional styles to modernist ones
insights.locator: It is also true that the dominant architectural styles

themes.theme: Historic demolition rates: the postwar era was not unusually destructive

insights.claim: Paris plans introduced in the 1950s foresaw demolishing two thirds of the city's blocks — the bulk of its nineteenth-century fabric — showing how radical postwar redevelopment ambitions were before conservation halted them.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Sets the counterfactual scale of central-city development capacity that conservation policy removed from the market.
insights.quote: plans for the city introduced in the 1950s foresaw the demolition of two thirds of Paris’s city blocks over the next few decades
insights.locator: In Paris, plans for the city introduced in the 1950s

insights.claim: Britain demolished at least 1.5 million homes in postwar slum clearance — nearly 10 percent of total housing stock, equating to fifteen to twenty percent of the prewar stock.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Benchmarks how much stock turnover a Western state was once politically able to execute, versus today's near-zero rate.
insights.quote: the government actually did demolish at least 1.5 million homes in slum clearance schemes in the postwar decades
insights.locator: In Britain, the government actually did demolish

insights.claim: Nearly half of the 12,000 buildings recorded in the 1933 Historic American Buildings Survey had been demolished or seriously mutilated by the mid-1960s, largely by privately led destruction.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Historical baseline showing US private redevelopment once ran far hotter than today's regulated environment permits.
insights.quote: nearly half of the 12,000 buildings recorded in the Historic American Buildings Survey of 1933 had been demolished or seriously mutilated by the middle of the 1960s
insights.locator: The United States seems to have had even higher rates

insights.claim: Modern demolition of old stock has collapsed to near zero: France demolished 1.8 percent of pre-1949 dwellings between 1999 and 2013 (0.13 percent annually), Berlin demolished just 9 pre-1919 buildings out of 50,337 in 2022 (0.018 percent), and North Rhine-Westphalia demolished 56 of 445,226 in 2023 (0.013 percent) — a pace that would take 7,951 years to clear its prewar stock.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Continental European prewar building stock is effectively permanent inventory — a hard supply ceiling for central urban real estate and a floor under prime land values.
insights.quote: At this rate, it will take North Rhine-Westphalia 7,951 years to demolish its prewar stock entirely.
insights.locator: In France, 1.8 percent of pre-1949 dwellings

insights.claim: Britain's count of pre-1919 dwellings actually rose between 2012 and 2024 because more homes were subdivided than demolished, an arithmetic sign that stock replacement has stopped entirely.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: UK housing supply growth now comes from subdivision and conversion rather than redevelopment — favoring refurbishment and PDR-style plays over ground-up in historic areas.
insights.quote: government statistics show a paradoxical increase in the number of pre-1919 dwellings between 2012 and 2024, the result of more homes being subdivided than demolished
insights.locator: In Britain, government statistics show

insights.claim: US demolition of old stock is higher than Europe's but still tiny — 0.25 percent annually for pre-1920 buildings in the Northeast and slightly over 0.3 percent in the West between 1997 and 2001 — partly because timber-framed American buildings are harder to keep safe.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Even the most permissive Western market recycles old stock at under a third of a percent a year, capping any redevelopment-led supply response.
insights.quote: in the American Northeast, the annual demolition rate of pre-1920 buildings between 1997 and 2001 was still only 0.25 percent, while in the West it was slightly over 0.3 percent
insights.locator: Old American buildings are demolished rather more often

insights.claim: Only 100 to 200 homes survive from the late-seventeenth-century City of London that once housed over half a million people, implying a destruction rate around 99.8 percent — considerably more thorough than the Great Fire of 1666 itself.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Peacetime market-driven redevelopment historically destroyed more stock than catastrophe — evidence that today's constraint is regulatory, not economic.
insights.quote: Assuming 100,000 homes in 1700 and two hundred survivors today, that means a destruction rate of 99.8 percent, considerably more thorough than that of the Great Fire.
insights.locator: London’s medieval stock was mostly destroyed

insights.claim: Roughly three quarters of Manhattan's several hundred Gilded Age urban palaces were demolished in a remarkably short period in the late 1920s — the Cornelius Vanderbilt II House in 1926 for Bergdorf Goodman, the Mrs William B Astor House in 1926 for Temple Emanu-El, and the Elbridge T Gerry Mansion in 1929 for the Pierre hotel — and all three replacements now carry heritage protection themselves.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Heritage designation is a moving frontier that ratchets outward over time — today's new build is tomorrow's protected asset, progressively shrinking the redevelopable land bank.
insights.quote: Ironically, all three of these buildings now have heritage protection, either as individual landmarks or as elements of historic districts.
insights.locator: In the Gilded Age, Manhattan had several hundred urban palaces

insights.claim: The absence of height restrictions in the United States, combined with the 1880s invention of elevators and steel frames, created intense incentives for rapid redevelopment — early skyscrapers like the Gillender (1897) and Home Insurance Building (1885) were themselves swiftly demolished for the larger Bankers Trust Building (1912) and Field Building (1934).
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Absent height caps, technology alone generates continuous stock turnover — the clearest historical proof that height limits, not economics, are the binding constraint today.
insights.quote: the lack of height restrictions created intense incentives for redevelopment after the invention of elevators and steel frames in the 1880s
insights.locator: This process was perhaps even more marked in the United States

insights.claim: Postwar modernists were in a sense less destructive than their predecessors, because they were halted after demolishing only a substantial minority of inherited stock while the Victorians and Georgians continued until they had torn down almost all of it.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Reframes the founding myth of the conservation movement, which matters for anyone arguing to loosen heritage rules on empirical grounds.
insights.quote: The idea that postwar planners were moved by destructive animus towards the past is mostly a myth.
insights.locator: The overall picture here is one of striking continuity

themes.theme: Why the 'conservation is a NIMBY pretext' theory fails

insights.claim: Conservation rules cannot be a NIMBY pretext because the sequencing is wrong: suburban zoning spread across Europe before 1914 and across North America between the wars, while conservation restrictions were minimal before the 1940s and only bound seriously in the 1960s and 70s — gaps of forty to seventy years.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Suggests YIMBY strategy that treats heritage as bad-faith cover is misdirected; heritage politics needs a separate, aesthetic-legitimacy playbook.
insights.quote: Why didn’t NIMBYs invent conservationism earlier? Why, indeed, did they bother to invent it in the 1960s, long after they had already succeeded in protecting their affluent suburbs from development using other arguments?
insights.locator: The most obvious problem is once again sequencing

insights.claim: One famous study found that the Blitz ultimately made London's economy 10 percent larger by enabling higher densities on former bomb sites — a result inexplicable under a pure NIMBY model, since randomly zeroing density should have lowered the baseline NIMBYs defend.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A natural experiment quantifying the GDP cost of heritage-driven density constraints; a 10 percent city-economy uplift is the order of magnitude at stake in central-city reform.
insights.quote: One famous study found that the Blitz ultimately made London’s economy 10 percent larger by enabling higher densities on former bomb sites.
insights.locator: Where European cities have densified their centers since 1945

insights.claim: The Lower Manhattan Expressway fight — over decayed manufacturing and warehouse areas in SoHo and Little Italy — drew support from national grandees including Eleanor Roosevelt, Lewis Mumford, Margaret Mead, Charles Abrams and William H Whyte, showing elite non-local mobilization rather than neighbor self-interest.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Landmark conservation battles are won by national reputational coalitions, meaning project risk scales with media salience rather than local sentiment.
insights.locator: Perhaps the most famous of all American conservationist battles

themes.theme: Urban form consequences: the L transect and the U transect

insights.claim: Cities where local NIMBYism is strong but heritage is scarce develop an 'L transect' — sheer skyscraper density at the core and flat low density everywhere else — as seen in Melbourne, Miami, Toronto, Calgary and Brisbane, versus the classic gradual 'urban transect'.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A city's transect shape is a readable signal of which regulatory constraint binds — CBD tower supply risk is high in L-transect cities while inner-ring land carries locked-up upside.
insights.quote: These cities have developed a distinctive ‘L transect’, sheer at the core but flat everywhere else.
insights.locator: Urbanists write about an ‘urban transect’

insights.claim: European city centers such as Paris, Rome and Madrid have been more perfectly frozen than any other neighborhood type, with building stock barely changed since 1960, forcing skyscraper districts onto low-end peripheral sites like Paris's La Défense and Madrid's AZCA.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: New European commercial density is confined to a handful of designated peripheral nodes — concentrating both supply and obsolescence risk in those specific submarkets.
insights.quote: the building stock of central Paris, Rome, or Madrid has hardly changed at all since 1960
insights.locator: By contrast, European city centers have been more perfectly frozen

insights.claim: If current plans for tall buildings around the Périphérique ring road proceed, Paris will end up with a 'U transect' — its highest densities displaced to the periphery rather than the center, inverting the normal economic geography of a city.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Watch Périphérique-adjacent zoning decisions as the main channel for new Paris density; peripheral land there is the option with real convexity.
insights.quote: Paris may end up with a gentle U transect, with its highest densities displaced to the periphery.
insights.locator: If current plans for tall buildings around the Périphérique

insights.claim: Nineteenth-century cities almost never cut railways through their historic cores — leaving London and Paris with rings of termini around the center — because steam and coal smoke made railways the one piece of infrastructure that era found overwhelmingly ugly.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Historical proof that perceived ugliness alone can block infrastructure even in permissive regimes — a lasting constraint on urban rail alignment and cost.
insights.quote: nineteenth-century people behaved just like twentieth-century people in respect of the one kind of infrastructure they found overwhelmingly ugly, just as the anti-ugliness theory would predict
insights.locator: There is one interesting exception to this destructiveness

themes.theme: Uglification as the true cause: modernism plus mass car ownership

insights.claim: Modernism — characterized by lack of ornament, repetitive facade patterns, and exposed steel and concrete — became dominant for everything except suburban housing in the 1950s, which is the main reason redevelopment switched from being aesthetically neutral to being perceived as uglifying.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific mechanism that turned redevelopment politically toxic — implying material and ornament choices carry political, not just cost, consequences.
insights.quote: This is the main reason that redevelopment switched from being aesthetically neutral to being uglifying.
insights.locator: How did people come to expect that new buildings would be uglier

insights.claim: Mass car ownership is the second cause of perceived uglification: cars are popular individually but degrade spaces collectively, turning nineteenth-century tree-lined boulevards with walking-pace carriages into modern highways that require sight and sound barriers.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Road-cutting-style infrastructure lost its historical aesthetic license, which is why urban highway projects are now near-impossible to consent in Western cities.
insights.quote: nobody prefers living near a modern highway, to the extent that the authorities often build sight and sound barriers around them
insights.locator: Second, at around the same time, mass car ownership

insights.claim: Redevelopment on former industrial or logistics sites remains widely popular today — cited examples being NOMA in Washington DC and Coal Drops Yard in London — showing that public opposition is to uglification specifically, not to redevelopment as such.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Brownfield and former-logistics sites are the lowest-political-risk development category in the West; underwrite them at tighter risk premia than historic-adjacent sites.
insights.quote: Even today, developments on former industrial or logistics sites are often widely popular, like NOMA in Washington DC or Coal Drops Yard in London.
insights.locator: Most people are not principled opponents of redevelopment as such

insights.claim: Conservation protection is overwhelmingly asymmetric by era: in England about 300 postwar buildings were listed as of 2003 growing to roughly 500 by 2015, out of some 375,000 listed buildings, while the American National Register applies a blanket 'fifty year rule' that almost never includes anything built in the last half century.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Postwar modernist stock is effectively unprotected and therefore the redevelopable inventory in constrained cities — a concrete screen for value-add sites.
insights.quote: In England, 300 postwar buildings had been listed as of 2003, apparently growing to about 500 in 2015, out of some 375,000 listed buildings in total.
insights.locator: There do exist conservation groups defending modernist architecture

insights.claim: Conservationists are argued to have sublimated an appreciation of beauty into an appreciation of age, secretly loving old buildings because they are beautiful while publicly claiming to love them because they are old, in order to avoid direct confrontation with high-status modernism and charges of pastiche-mongering.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: If true, the binding political constraint is aesthetic rather than historical — meaning beautiful new construction could eventually unlock conservation-frozen land in a way historical arguments never will.
insights.quote: many conservationists secretly love old buildings because they are beautiful, while pretending to love them because they are old
insights.locator: It also seems to me that the anti-ugliness theory

insights.claim: Georgians and Victorians assumed ordinary houses depreciated with use like cars or computers today, so a new replacement was presumed better — an attitude captured by The Builder in 1868 celebrating the replacement of Georgian street building by a new Victorian London.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Building depreciation was once the default cultural assumption; its reversal into appreciation-through-age is the root of today's land-value distortion in historic cores.
insights.quote: normal houses generally declined in value over time, like cars or computers today: the default assumption was that buildings degraded with use, and hence that a new replacement was probably better
insights.locator: On the other hand, many Georgians and Victorians thought

insights.claim: The conservation movement's timing is decisive evidence: developers demolished vast quantities of historic stock for thousands of years with barely a whisper of resistance, then within ten or fifteen years of an unpopular style becoming ascendant an immense halt-the-replacement movement appeared almost from nowhere.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The core causal claim of the essay; if right, aesthetic policy is a first-order lever on Western housing supply rather than a decorative afterthought.
insights.quote: then, within ten or fifteen years of the ascendancy of an architectural style that the public disliked, an immense movement to halt the replacement of old buildings appeared almost from nowhere
insights.locator: The anti-ugliness theory of conservationism lines up

themes.theme: How much conservation actually costs housing supply

insights.claim: Only about a fifth of housing in Europe's oldest-stock countries dates from before 1919, and just 6 percent in the United States, so raw statistics suggest heritage rules should barely constrain new construction.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The naive share statistic understates the constraint — do not size heritage risk by stock percentage.
insights.quote: Even in the European countries with the oldest build stock, only a fifth of housing dates from before 1919, while in the United States just 6 percent does.
insights.locator: How much impact does conservation have on the housing shortage?

insights.claim: Conservation's real bite comes from concentration plus spillover: historic buildings cluster in city centers and conservation systems restrict what can be done in the environs of old buildings as well as within their curtilages, so most European city centers are effectively solid phalanxes of conservation designations that displace new development to inferior peripheral sites.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Setting/curtilage rules are the underappreciated policy lever — reforming them, not delisting buildings, is what would release central European development sites.
insights.quote: in most European cities, centers are effectively solid phalanxes of conservation designations, with new development largely displaced to inferior sites on the urban periphery
insights.locator: But because historic buildings are concentrated in city centers

insights.claim: Mapping Paris by pre-1914 buildings alone shows that, given restrictions on development in the settings of historic buildings, only a handful of sites remain available for development within the entire city.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Intra-Paris development supply is close to exhausted, structurally supporting central Paris asset prices and rents regardless of demand policy.
insights.quote: this means that only a handful of sites remain for possible development within the city
insights.locator: Paris with only buildings from before 1914 marked

insights.claim: US conservation impact is smaller than Europe's but still considerable: Manhattan, central Boston and San Francisco lack blanket designations like Paris, Amsterdam, Madrid or Rome, yet large areas fall under conservation protections that map onto exactly the places YIMBYs most want to develop.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Heritage overlays in high-productivity US cores are a targeted, mappable constraint — screen sites against designation maps before underwriting upzoning optionality.
insights.quote: the historic stock that does exist is heavily concentrated in the most economically vital places
insights.locator: The impact of conservation in the United States is smaller

insights.claim: Prohousing advocates have secured important victories in overriding local zoning control at state and national level, but have almost invariably failed to enable more development in historic areas — a consistent pattern across reform campaigns worldwide.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: State preemption trades work on suburbs but not on heritage; do not price heritage-area upzoning into reform-driven land theses.
insights.quote: But one area where they have almost invariably failed is in enabling more development in historic areas.
insights.locator: Today, American prohousing advocates work to generate

insights.claim: Because people feel that the stock of beautiful buildings is finite and irreplaceable, no economic or transport argument will ever win permission for large-scale demolition of historic stock — the constraint can only be broken by restoring confidence that change is not disfigurement.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Implies the binding leading indicator for central-city supply is design and style policy, not economic modeling or transport appraisal — monitor design codes and pattern books rather than viability studies.
insights.quote: If that curse can be broken, it will not be by the arguments of economists and transport planners, but by confidence that change is not disfigurement, and that it will yield cities we can love.
insights.locator: For most Westerners today, however
